La vente sur les marchés, un autre visag: Market Sales, Another Face of Seasonal Agricultural Workers
« J’aimerais revenir l’année prochaine,: “I’d like to come back next year, if the boss asks me again, then I’ll come back here with them”
Des rythmes <em>latinos</em> s’échappent: Latino rhythms spill out of a flower stall at Atwater Market, a salsa, to be precise. At the entrance of a mini greenhouse filled with plants of different sizes and colours, Rubén, a Mexican seasonal worker, unloads a few boxes and takes instructions from his boss.
C’est une journée chaude et humide de ju: It’s a hot, humid July day in Montréal. The high season for selling flowers and plants is behind us; it usually runs from mid-May to June. Rubén still puts his knowledge of plants to good use. Every day, he loads and unloads the precious merchandise.
Rubén, un travailleur saisonnier mexicai: Rubén, a Mexican seasonal worker, is employed at Atwater Market. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
« En juin, on en voit plus », assure-t-i: “You see more of them in June,” he says when asked whether there are many seasonal agricultural workers at Atwater Market. No one knows exactly how many of them, who come to Quebec to work in the fields and on farms, also sell to the public. Until now, it was not common to see their faces at the market. At least not in customer service. It’s also the first time Rubén has been asked to work in flower sales, which makes him very happy.
« C’est difficile de savoir pourquoi ils: “It’s hard to know why they chose me,” he says with humility. “This is my first year working at Atwater, even though I’ve been coming to Canada for nine years. Maybe my bosses saw that I had a chance of doing well here. Usually I’m in the greenhouses. I was there from January to May,” explains Rubén, who works in long sleeves, jeans and a cap even when the thermometer reads 30°C.
<strong>Des travailleurs agricoles de pl: More and more farm workers at the markets
La présence de travailleurs agricoles sa: The presence of seasonal agricultural workers at the markets is not surprising given the current labour shortage in the service sector and the growing number of them coming to Quebec. According to Statistics Canada, the number of temporary foreign workers in the agricultural sector who came to the province rose by 64% between 2020 and 2022, from 13,094 to 21,531.
Rubén, lui, est venu au Québec en passan: Rubén came to Quebec through the Seasonal Agricultural Worker Program (SAWP), with an “open” work permit valid until December. He says his working conditions are good, both in the greenhouses and at the market. He nevertheless prefers going to Atwater, because he considers the arrangement beneficial for everyone.
« Parce que nous apprenons d’eux, les tr: “Because we learn from them, the local or Quebec workers, and they learn from the experience we have in the greenhouses. For example, what the plant is called, how long it lasts, how many times it needs to be watered, what you have to give it to survive if it’s sick? All of that,” he explains.
Ce qu’il apprécie le plus dans cette nou: What he appreciates most about this new role is gaining skills, especially a command of French. “I learn as much in the greenhouses as at the market. But here, I learn to manage on my own more. I’m starting to speak and understand a little. I’d like to learn a bit more so the customer leaves satisfied with what he tells me and what I’m trying to tell him,” he says with a smile.
Claude Wilson est le propriétaire du kio: Claude Wilson owns the stall where Rubén works. He is the son of Noël and Rita Wilson, founders of Wilson et fils, a business that started in 1957 and began harvesting annual flowers in 1978. The farm is located in Saint-Rémi, 40 minutes south of Montréal.
« Il y a des travailleurs mexicains et g: “There are Mexican and Guatemalan workers… They work very well, especially considering the working conditions. It’s lucky that they’re happy to be here,” he says.
Un portrait de Claude Wilson. Photo: Pab: A portrait of Claude Wilson. Photo: Pablo Ortiz
S’il affirme que la pénurie de main-d’œu: While he says the labour shortage pushed him to employ seasonal agricultural workers at the market, he also explains that he needs employees who can carry heavy crates and move plants.
« Habituellement, ce sont surtout les fe: “Usually it’s mostly the women who are there to sell the flowers, while the other employees set up the stock and water the plants. When they’re done, they come and lend a hand. They’re people who think ahead. But I have to say: the ones who are there are there because they like it, because they know how to talk to people, because they help each other and because they also make the effort to speak French. If they don’t feel comfortable with the public, they’re better off in the greenhouses. It works very well because, as you can see, they like what they do,” says Claude Wilson.
Simón* travaille dans un kiosque de légu: Simón* has been working at a vegetable stall at Jean-Talon Market for about twenty days. He arrived in Canada in April. At the market, his colleagues are all women. Like Rubén, he is in charge of the heavy work at the stall, but he is also in contact with customers, which allows him to learn and practise French.
« Je viens au Canada depuis deux saisons: “I’ve been coming to Canada for two seasons already, but this is the first time I’m working at the market,” he says in a reserved tone. “I was told I had to come, especially to carry the heavy loads. But I always work with the public, I sell vegetables. I feel very good here, because it’s something totally different,” says the employee, who is also Mexican.
Pour l’instant, il a un objectif clair :: For now, he has one clear goal: to learn French. “That’s what interests me most,” he adds. There are days when he still works in the fields, on the farma, a term farm workers use to refer to farms. “I work at everything, especially harvesting,” he explains.
Au marché, Simón dit qu’il s’en sort trè: At the market, Simón says he’s doing very well. “I get along very well with everyone, there’s a good atmosphere. I think they brought me here because they saw that I worked well, so they gave me the chance to take a test. If I worked with the same drive, I could continue, and that’s what I did. It’s a different environment,” he explains.
Pour se rendre à Jean-Talon, Simón voyag: To get to Jean-Talon, Simón travels with his bosses every day from the farm, which is an hour from Montréal. “I work from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. and I’m paid minimum wage. On this farm, we work with about fifteen temporary foreign workers, and there are Mexicans and Guatemalans,” he explains.

<strong>Passion pour le travail avec le: A passion for working with the public
José Luis travaille quant à lui aux <em>: José Luis, for his part, has been working at Serres Riel Inc for a few weeks, a business that also has a presence at Atwater Market. Like Rubén, he has already had the chance this year to work in customer service. He will be able to work there until September.
Au départ, il s’est rendu au marché pour: At first, he went to the market to do the heavy work. “I had to replace what customers bought. For example, if they bought three geraniums, I had to bring three geraniums, and so on with all the products, the pots, the balcony planters.”
Il a eu une petite expérience au marché: He had a brief experience at Atwater Market three years ago, and since then he has discovered a passion for working with the public. He first came to Canada five years ago through the TFWP and has worked for Les Serres Riel Inc. for four years.
« Le marché est très spécial pour moi »,: “The market is very special to me,” he says with a charisma he displays throughout the interview. “I’ve always had a good relationship with people. I find my work more interesting when I’m with the public. I’ve learned a bit of French. My boss’s sister, who is my direct boss, doesn’t speak Spanish, and that helps me make an effort to learn the language,” he adds.
José Luis, lui aussi mexicain, estime qu: José Luis, who is also Mexican, believes that working at Atwater has helped him understand customers’ needs, particularly when it comes to choosing and caring for plants and flowers. “And it’s the place where, little by little, I’ve been able to practise my French more. That’s where I learned to speak more.”
José Luis dit qu’il apprécie travailler: José Luis says he enjoys working at Atwater Market (Photo: courtesy of José Luis).
Les <em>Serres Riel Inc</em>., situés à: Serres Riel Inc., located in Saint-Rémi, employs about twenty seasonal agricultural workers, and this year four of them, all Mexican, work at Atwater Market. Most of the time, they are in charge of moving plants and other items, but José Luis explains that it was his thirst to learn that led him to work on the sales side of the business. “The person in charge of the stall saw that I was doing good work, and that’s why he put me in sales. When there was a staff shortage, they sent me to fill that position,” he explains.
Rubén, Simón et José Luis gagnent le sal: Rubén, Simón and José Luis earn minimum wage, set at $15.25 an hour in Quebec. Whether they’re at the market, in the fields or in the greenhouses, they get one day off every two weeks, which they use to send money to their families. All three are married, and their wives and children live in Mexico.
« J’aimerais revenir l’année prochaine,: “I’d like to come back next year, if the boss asks me again, then I’ll come back here with them,” Simón answers when we ask him whether he’d like to keep working at Jean-Talon Market.
Rubén, lui, aimerait retourner travaille: Rubén would like to return to work for the same company in 2024 and have the chance to keep serving customers at the market.
Un souhait que José Luis partage égaleme: José Luis shares that wish. “I’ve always told my colleagues that I went to the market to work hard, so that they’d take me back. Next year, I intend to go back.”
Tous trois aimeraient devenir des réside: All three would like to become permanent residents of Canada and bring their families with them. But that status is hard for them to obtain in Quebec. Indeed, François Legault’s government has restricted seasonal agricultural workers’ access to the Quebec Experience Program, a pathway the province offers temporary workers and international students to obtain permanent residency.
Malgré les énormes sacrifices qu’ils con: Despite the enormous sacrifices they make, year after year, living for long periods far from their families, their homes and their culture, the three Mexican workers say they are satisfied with what they have accomplished so far.
Apercevoir les visages des travailleurs: Seeing the faces of seasonal agricultural workers, hearing their accents, seeing their hands and their sun-browned skin in commonly frequented places like Montréal’s markets gives a new glimpse of how important these workers are. Rubbing shoulders with them, instead of only seeing their photos in the fields, may be another way of showing the great contribution of these people who, although they spend more time here than in their home countries, continue to be temporary workers.
